chief_complaint: excruciating sharp eye pain, tearing, foreign body sensation, and photophobia immediately after being poked in eye by toddler
hpi_details: 32M presenting with severe pain, tearing, and blepharospasm after fingernail poke where fluorescein examination under cobalt blue light reveals a sharply demarcated green fluorescent epithelial defect without stromal infiltrate responding to topical erythromycin ointment and bandage contact lens.
ideas: He thinks a tiny piece of his toddler's fingernail broke off and is still lodged under his eyelid scratching his eyeball.
concerns: He is worried that bacteria from his toddler's dirty hands will cause an infection that permanently scars his eye and damages his eyesight.
expectations: He hopes the doctor can flush out any remaining nail fragment and prescribe numbing drops so he can keep his eye open.

available_results.value: Sharply demarcated fluorescent corneal epithelial defect without stromal infiltrate
available_results.note: Consistent with an uncomplicated corneal abrasion after open-globe injury is excluded.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Corneal abrasion (fingernail trauma) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Corneal abrasion (fingernail trauma) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Corneal Abrasion Fingernail Trauma, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: excruciating sharp eye pain, tearing, foreign body sensation, and photophobia immediately after being poked in eye by toddler

Key HPI features: 32M presenting with severe pain, tearing, and blepharospasm after fingernail poke where fluorescein examination under cobalt blue light reveals a sharply demarcated green fluorescent epithelial defect without stromal infiltrate responding to topical erythromycin ointment and bandage contact lens.

Objective/Exam findings: Assess visual acuity, pupils, extraocular movements, and fluorescein staining after excluding an open globe. This case shows a sharply demarcated fluorescein-positive epithelial defect without stromal infiltrate, consistent with a corneal abrasion.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Corneal abrasion (fingernail trauma).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Corneal foreign body without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any stromal infiltrate would suggest infection rather than simple abrasion.
management_principles: Exclude open-globe injury and retained foreign body; obtain urgent ophthalmology assessment for reduced vision, infiltrate, hyphema, abnormal pupil, or concern for penetration
For an uncomplicated non-contact-lens abrasion, provide oral analgesia, topical prophylactic antibiotic ointment, and 24- to 48-hour follow-up; avoid dispensing topical anesthetics for home use
Avoid patching; return immediately for worsening pain, reduced vision, discharge, or failure to improve
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: 32M with sharp eye pain, tearing, and photophobia after being poked in the eye by a toddler's fingernail.
red_flags: Any stromal infiltrate would suggest infection rather than simple abrasion

must_ask.say: Can you describe exactly how the poke happened and what touched your eye?
How severe is the pain, and does light make it worse?
Does it feel like something is still in your eye?
Did anything sharp or with force go deeply into the eye, or was it just a light poke?

must_ask.objective: Explain the fluorescein exam and treatment plan
must_ask.say: We'll stain your eye with a special dye to see the scratch, then give you antibiotic ointment.

history.answer: My right eye hurts terribly and will not stop watering after my toddler poked me in the eye with his finger this morning.
It happened about two hours ago while playing with my son, and the intense pain and tearing started the moment he poked me.
It is only in my right eye. My left eye feels completely normal, aside from some sympathetic tearing.
The entire white part of my right eye turned red right away, especially around the colored iris.
It is an excruciating, sharp pain that I would rate a 9 out of 10. It aches constantly and stings sharply whenever I try to blink.
Yes, it constantly feels like there is a piece of grit or an eyelash trapped under my eyelid that I cannot wash out.
My vision is slightly blurry from the flood of tears, but when I dab them away I can still read letters and see clearly.
Yes, even normal indoor room light makes my eye ache and water, so I have to keep it squeezed shut.
No, I do not see any halos or rainbow rings around lights, and I have no headache, nausea, or vomiting.
There is constant clear, watery tearing streaming down my cheek, but no thick yellow pus or crusty discharge.
No, it does not itch at all. It just burns and throbs with sharp pain.
The eyelids are mildly puffy from all the tears, and the muscle keeps spasming shut involuntarily.
Moving my eye stings because the eyelid rubs against it, but there is no deep pain behind the eye, no bulging, no double vision, and no fever.
history.topic: Pain with eye movement or fever

history.answer: No, I have not had a cold, runny nose, or sore throat recently, and no one around me has had pink eye.
I have never worn contact lenses. I only use reading glasses occasionally when working on the computer.
My two-year-old son was sitting on my lap waving his hands, and his fingernail jabbed straight into my open right eye.
It was strictly a soft toddler fingernail while playing. There were no metal fragments, glass, wood splinters, or high-speed objects.
No, I do not suffer from seasonal allergies, allergic rhinitis, asthma, or eczema.
No, I have never had chronic dry eyes, dry mouth, or eye fatigue before this accident.
No, I have no morning lower back stiffness, swollen joints, mouth sores, or bowel problems.
No, I have never had shingles, cold sores, or any fluid-filled bumps on my forehead or nose.
No, I do not take aspirin or blood thinners, and I have not had any violent coughing, vomiting, or heavy lifting.
I have never had any previous eye conditions, glaucoma, eye surgery, or recurrent episodes like this.
My toddler poked me right in the eye, and it feels like a broken piece of his nail is still stuck inside scraping around.
Toddlers touch everything, so I'm really scared his dirty fingernail carried germs that will scar my cornea and ruin my vision.
I'm hoping you can check if any piece of nail is still in there, wash it out, and give me some numbing drops so I can actually open my eye.
I have high blood pressure and slightly elevated cholesterol, but both are well managed.
I had my appendix removed when I was seventeen, but I have had no other operations or hospital stays.
I take lisinopril 10 milligrams once daily in the morning for my blood pressure. I have not put any drops or ointments in my eye today.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or latex.
I am a non-smoker and have never used tobacco or nicotine products.
I drink one or two beers on the weekend with friends, but nothing during the work week.
I work as an accountant at an office, and I live with my wife and our two-year-old son.
My father has high blood pressure, but there is no family history of glaucoma, vision loss, or genetic eye disease.

exam.finding: The patient is alert, grimacing, and holding his right eye tightly shut due to blepharospasm and photophobia.
Blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, heart rate is 78 beats/min, respiratory rate is 16 breaths/min, body temperature is 36.6 C, and oxygen saturation is 99% on ambient air.
The right eye displays prominent conjunctival injection and ciliary flush with profuse clear tearing, with no subconjunctival hemorrhage or purulent discharge.

Visual acuity is 20/25 in the right eye and 20/20 in the left eye; pupils are equal, round, and reactive without afferent defect; fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light demonstrates a sharply demarcated corneal epithelial defect without stromal infiltrate; upper eyelid eversion shows no retained foreign body.
Periorbital skin and facial dermatomes are intact without vesicles, swelling, lacerations, or rash.
